title: Morphology-resolved scrambling in a chaotic quantum billiard
abstract: Chaotic quantum systems can retain spatial memory through scarred eigenstates, but whether these static structures control scrambling remains unclear. This work establishes a morphology-resolved connection between scarred eigenstates and eigenstate-resolved OTOCs in a peanut-shaped quantum billiard. Scalar localisation diagnostics, including differential entropy and continuum participation ratios, detect anomalous concentration but discard spatial architecture. A scale-normalised density overlap, in contrast, directly compares probability density profiles, revealing families of orthogonal eigenstates with nearly identical spatial morphology. Comparing the complete OTOC time traces of these orthogonal eigenstates reveals that morphological recurrence has dynamical content: moderate density overlap yields no universal prediction, whereas strongly recurring morphologies exhibit nearly identical OTOC growth and saturation. Thus, scarred structures act as spatial templates for operator growth, not merely static violations of ergodicity. This morphology-resolved framework turns eigenstate shape into a quantitative predictor of scrambling and provides a scale-controlled diagnostic of weak ergodicity breaking in quantum chaos.
summary: The paper connects the static spatial structure of wave functions in chaotic quantum systems to their dynamic scrambling behavior. By developing a density overlap metric, the authors group eigenstates by shared morphology rather than just energy or localization. They show that strong morphological recurrence constrains and predicts the growth rate of information scrambling measured via OTOCs.
main_problem: The work investigates whether static structural features, like scarred eigenstates, in chaotic quantum systems provide a quantitative prediction for the dynamics of information scrambling.
main_result: Strong morphological recurrence among orthogonal eigenstates leads to nearly identical Out-of-Time-Order Correlator (OTOC) growth and saturation, suggesting that eigenstate shape acts as a spatial template constraining scrambling dynamics.
method: The authors developed a morphology-resolved diagnostic using scale-normalized density overlap ($S(n, m)$) to group eigenstates by shared probability density profiles, which were then correlated with OTOC time traces.
model_or_system: The study uses a theoretical model of a quantum billiard shaped like a peanut ($\Omega_{	ext{peanut}}$), representing a chaotic system where wave functions exhibit scarring due to unstable classical orbits.
key_observables: Scale-normalized density overlap ($S(n, m)$), eigenstate-resolved OTOCs, and the resulting curve distance/similarity metrics for comparing time evolution.
important_parameters: The degree of morphological recurrence (high $S(n, m)$) is crucial; the relationship between morphology and dynamics is found to be threshold-like.
main_assumptions: Standard localization diagnostics (entropy, IPR) are insufficient because they only measure concentration and discard spatial architecture. The analysis assumes that OTOCs capture the relevant scrambling dynamics.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate classical trajectories alongside eigenstate intensities in the billiard; one figure summarizes scalar diagnostics, while others compare density overlap matrices with corresponding OTOC time traces to show correlation.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the limitations of standard localization measures. It then introduces and applies the morphology-resolved diagnostic ($S(n, m)$) to group states. Finally, it correlates these morphological classes by comparing their full OTOC time evolution to demonstrate a quantitative link between static shape and dynamic scrambling.
why_interesting: This work provides a novel way to connect geometric/structural properties (morphology) directly to non-equilibrium dynamics (scrambling), offering a powerful diagnostic tool for quantum chaos beyond simple ergodicity measures.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Classical trajectories and eigenstate intensities in the peanut-shaped billiard. Top: coloured curves mark selected slowly diverging orbits, while the white dashed curve indi- cates chaotic motion. Bottom: eigenstate intensities ψ(x)2 show enhanced probability density along the corresponding classical structures. The colour coding connects each eigen- state morphology to the corresponding classical structure in the upper panel.

FIG. 2. Eigenstate morphology and scar diagnostics across the spectrum. Top: representative intensity profiles |ψ|2, with colours matching the highlighted data points. Bottom: spectral variation of (a) Differential Shannon entropy HS, (b) IPR, (c) DKL, and (d) nPR versus eigenstate index n. Insets display a few selected eigenstate probability densities. While these scalar diagnostics reveal anomalous concentrations and deviations from ergodic spatial filling, they collapse each eigenstate to a single number and therefore cannot resolve whether distinct eigenstates share the same spatial morphology.

FIG. 2(c & d) present dimensionless diagnostics that remove this ambiguity by using dimensionless, scale- independent measures. The KL divergence highlights de- viations from the uniform density, so localised or scarred eigenstates appear as large positive outliers. The nPR rescales the participation ratio by the billiard area and therefore measures the fraction of the domain effectively

FIG. 3. Density-overlap similarity between eigenstates. (a) Thresholded matrix S(n, m) ≥0.61, where off-diagonal elements near unity identify distinct eigenstates with nearly identical probability densities. (b) Network of spatially similar eigenstates, with edges drawn for S(n, m) ≥0.67; edge colour and thickness encode S(n, m). The balloon layout is only visual. (c) Eigenstates most similar to the reference state n = 71; the red line marks Sth = 0.61.

FIG. 4. Morphology-resolved OTOC dynamics. (a-e) show eigenstate groups Gg with similar density morphology, iden- tified by the overlap S(n, m). Grey curves are individual OTOCs and coloured curves are group averages Cavg g (t). Den- sity thumbnails show representative members from the cor- responding morphology class. (f) compares averaged curves across all classes, demonstrating that recurring eigenstate morphologies yield distinct yet internally consistent OTOC growth and saturation profiles.
